articles.title: Yes, I enjoyed the other 46 points, too
articles.dek: Mara Voss on a 49–3 win, a returner who kept skipping the commute, and the perfectly reasonable pleasure of watching Mossdeep stay unbeaten.
articles.author: mara-voss

body.text: I spent last week worrying about what Mossdeep would lose without Tyran Armstead. Then the Eclipse won 49–3. You may imagine that this has made me reluctant to revisit my concerns. On the contrary, I have prepared a very balanced response: forty-nine points, three allowed, please leave the arithmetic on the screen.

Marshall Flock returned two kickoffs for touchdowns. Marino threw three more. Ninjaskamara and Ninjulio supplied the rushing scores. There were enough ways into the end zone that the defense could have requested a quieter afternoon and still received one. I enjoyed it. I don't intend to disguise that enjoyment as an advanced statistical conclusion.

Last week's column asked what survives a missing piece. The answer against Fuchsia was quite a lot. The protection allowed one sack, Marino completed eighteen of twenty-three passes, and Mossdeep never needed to turn the game into a referendum on one absent tackle. Armstead is now clear of the injury report. The test was useful. Getting him back is useful, too.

I also remember Dewford. A week earlier, Mossdeep needed a late field goal to win 23–20. The Breakers subsequently beat Cinnabar. Anyone trying to sell the Eclipse's narrow escape as proof of an ordinary team has acquired an inconvenient additional result. Dewford looked capable against Mossdeep and kept looking capable afterward. That is how a close win can improve with age.
Permission to enjoy a good thing

Five-and-zero is a lovely record. A scoring margin of plus-163 makes it lovelier. The Eclipse have scored 203 points and allowed forty. These are actual things that happened, and I would like to spend a paragraph enjoying them before somebody asks how well a kickoff return predicts the next kickoff return.

It doesn't have to predict anything to have won this game. Flock's 95-yard return answered Fuchsia's field goal with twenty-four seconds left in the first quarter. His 93-yard return opened the second half. Between them, the visitors experienced the peculiar discomfort of kicking off twice and immediately defending an extra point twice. I imagine the next kickoff felt longer than usual.

Flock was credited with 314 return yards on eight returns. The touchdowns are the obvious feature. The whole total matters because field position changes what the offense is asked to do. An efficient quarterback becomes more troublesome when the return game keeps offering him a shorter assignment. On Sunday, two of those assignments were reduced to watching.

The offense still did its own work. Gronkaludon caught five passes for 87 yards and a touchdown. Driflon Diggs caught seven for 73 and two scores. Ninjaskamara ran for 94 yards on ten attempts. There was no shortage of players prepared to fill the part of the scoreboard Flock had left for them.

body.speaker: Marshall Flock
body.text: I liked the first return. Then there was another kickoff. I tried to make that one useful, too.

That is an exceptionally mild description of a very rude afternoon for the Shadows. Docile is a nature; it isn't a promise to return the ball politely. I appreciate a player who can provide explosive plays without needing to narrate every yard afterward. The rest of us can handle the narrating. Some of us have considerable energy available for it.
A few matters for next week

Lavaridge comes to Mossdeep after losing 48–0 to Saffron. I expect the Eclipse to win. There, a prediction in ordinary language. I will not bury it under six conditional clauses until it becomes impossible to grade. If Mossdeep can't protect its quarterback and move the ball against this opponent, I'll have something less pleasant to write next week.

The checkable part is simple. Keep Marino upright, get productive early downs, and avoid turning the ball over to an opponent that badly needs help. I want to see the offense sustain drives even if the return game declines to score fourteen points. It is unreasonable to assign Flock two kickoff touchdowns every week. It is reasonable to ask the offense to remain good without them.

The defense has a particularly appealing chance to make Lavaridge's week longer. Saffron sacked Delphox four times. Mossdeep recorded four sacks against Fuchsia. That doesn't make the next total automatic, but it gives us a clear matchup to watch: can the Inferno keep their passer out of the long-yardage situations that fed Saffron's rush? If they can't, the Eclipse should have opportunities.

Electric Berry recovered a fumble and intercepted a pass against Fuchsia. Clay Rathews supplied two sacks. There are times when a defense's statistics become a long list of people enjoying the same afternoon. This was one of them. The useful question next week is whether the pressure and the tackling arrive before the game has become comfortable.

I don't need another 49–3 to believe Mossdeep belongs near the top of the league. I do need the ordinary parts to remain dependable: protection, possession, field position, finishing drives. A spectacular return can hide a stalled possession. A huge margin can make a loose quarter seem harmless. The pleasure of watching this team is that it has given us enough good football to discuss those details from first place.

Mt. Silver is unbeaten, too, and Saffron's defense is making an aggressive claim on everyone's attention. The competition is real. Mossdeep's case is real as well. Five wins, forty points allowed, and an offense with several ways to hurt a team is a very persuasive beginning.

So yes, I'll watch the protection next week. I'll watch the third downs and the injury report and all the things a responsible person should watch. I also reserve the right to enjoy a kickoff return that removes the need for any of those things for the next ninety-three yards. Flock has earned an audience. At five-and-zero, Mossdeep has earned one, too.

art.alt: Marshall Flock, Swellow No. 44, in Mossdeep magenta and gold on a kickoff return.

articles.title: Twelve carries? Cinnabar, pick up the ball
articles.dek: Dorian Pike has run out of patience with an offense that asked for another passing rescue and got a 23–16 loss in Dewford.
articles.author: dorian-pike

body.text: Twelve carries. Twenty-five rushing yards. There is your Cinnabar column, delivered early enough that someone might still use it. The Blaze went to Dewford, lost 23–16, and supplied the defense with another afternoon of waiting for the offense to decide whether it intended to possess the football for more than a philosophical moment.

I am furious because this team is good enough to make the fury worthwhile. Cinnabar is 3–2 with a plus-37 scoring margin. It can throw. It can defend. It can produce a game that looks perfectly manageable in the third quarter and still leave me staring at a fourth-down completion that wasn't remotely long enough. That last talent requires considerably less encouragement.

Exploud caught six passes for 97 yards and a touchdown. The quarterback threw for 223 yards. The Blaze led 16–10 after a third-quarter field goal. Nobody was being asked to climb out of an impossible hole. Cinnabar had a lead, time and an opportunity to make Dewford chase. It finished by chasing a touchdown itself.

The Breakers ran 36 times for 149 yards. Cinnabar ran twelve times for 25. Yes, those are different offenses. Yes, passing can be productive. I am aware of the modern world. I would also like my team to do something useful on the ground before its entire afternoon depends on another throw finding another receiver while the clock becomes everybody's least favorite participant.
The lead was there

Exploud's 28-yard touchdown catch gave Cinnabar a 13–10 lead with 5:11 left in the third. The next scoring drive produced a 36-yard field goal and a six-point advantage. At that stage, there was a perfectly serviceable route to a road win. Stop Dewford, possess the ball, add points if possible. The directions fit on a small card.

Dewford made a 44-yard field goal late in the quarter. The Blaze still led 16–13. Their next drive went fifty yards in ten plays and ended on downs with 4:55 remaining. Fifty yards of effort, no points, and a short interval before the defense was asked to return. This is the kind of drive that gets called promising by people who didn't need it to pay anything.

The Breakers answered with thirteen plays and 74 yards. Unfezant finished it with a ten-yard touchdown reception at 2:08. Cinnabar's six-point lead had become a four-point deficit. There is no mysterious explanation in the middle. Dewford assembled the drive it needed. The Blaze failed to stop it.

Then came the interception. Meowscarada returned it seventeen yards, and Dewford made a 37-yard field goal with 1:38 left. Now Cinnabar needed seven. A game the Blaze had led by six had become a one-drive emergency. I have seen enough emergencies in which the first suggestion is to ask the passer for a miracle. I would like a different departmental procedure.

The last possession began with a sack by Kricketune. Seven yards lost. Two incompletions followed, with Gumshoos and Mawile recording breakups. On fourth-and-seventeen, the completion to Wigglytuff gained seven. The arithmetic was accurate and absolutely useless. Dewford took over with 1:07 left and ended it.
The useful anger

I'm not going to demand forty runs because I am annoyed by twelve. A bad running play remains a bad running play if you perform it with conviction. The useful demand is that Cinnabar build a credible way to gain yards without asking the passing game to solve every difficult down. Twenty-five rushing yards doesn't make a defense spend much time worrying about the alternative.

A defense that can concentrate on the passer gets to make the obvious problem worse. The late sack wasn't merely seven yards. It changed the whole final possession, leaving Cinnabar trying to recover distance before it could pursue the first down. By the time the fourth-down throw arrived, seven yards had become an invitation to surrender the ball.

The Blaze also need to finish the drives they do extend. Ten plays and fifty yards should have been a chance to make Dewford's required answer more demanding. Instead, the Breakers needed one touchdown to lead. This is why I can't be satisfied by the passing yardage or Exploud's excellent day. Productive stretches have to purchase something.

I still like this offense's ability to create a long completion. Exploud demonstrated it. I still like a team that has scored 98 points while allowing 61. Those are reasons to demand better, not reasons to waive the complaint. Cinnabar has already shown enough capability that this loss feels avoidable rather than inevitable. That distinction is precisely what makes it so irritating.

Pewter comes next. The Rockers just won 12–10 on four field goals. They will happily accept a game in which every Cinnabar possession expires before it reaches the end zone. The Blaze should be able to ask more difficult questions than Rustboro did through the air. They also need to protect the ball well enough that Unown isn't handed another afternoon of manageable assignments.

I want an early lead and an offense that behaves as though it knows what to do with one. I want the fourth quarter to contain a productive possession before the final emergency. I want the running game to register as something more than the quiet space between passing attempts. These are not extravagant requests for a club that considers itself a contender.

Cinnabar can beat Pewter. I expect it to. If the Blaze give me another useful-looking loss and twelve ornamental carries, the next column will be less polite. I recognize that some readers may find that threat difficult to distinguish from the current column. Watch the rushing total. I'll make the difference clear.

art.alt: Cinnabar orange and gold helmet beside a football on stadium turf.

articles.title: The trade was completed. The explanation is still due.
articles.dek: Ellis Quill on Milotic’s extraordinary return, Sunyshore’s first defeat, and the danger of letting one afternoon write the whole transaction history.
articles.author: ellis-quill

body.text: Milotic made the trade story wonderfully easy to tell and rather harder to evaluate. Sunyshore sent him to Violet in Week 5. Against his former team, he returned an interception for a touchdown, forced and recovered a fumble, and finished as the defensive player of the game. Violet won 33–20. If you were designing a memorable first chapter, restraint would probably have prevented you from using all of that.

The first chapter is real. The final judgment isn't available yet. I expect that distinction to survive approximately three seconds of discussion, because nobody who watched Milotic run fifty-two yards with Jolt Vick's pass wants to begin by discussing the rest of the package. I don't particularly want to begin there either. The cornerback earned the opening paragraph.

What interests me is the pressure this puts on Sunyshore's explanation. The Starseekers were unbeaten. They traded six players for four. One of the departures then supplied the clearest difference in their first loss. A manager can have a defensible plan and still endure a dreadful afternoon. This was a very public test of that possibility.

The actual outgoing group was Audino, Milotic, Frillish, Minccino, Poltchageist and Numel. Violet sent Buizel, Eelektrik, Anorith and Slakoth. There were no picks. Those names matter because a six-for-four exchange can't honestly be reduced to one cornerback forever, even when that cornerback makes the first game feel like a personal editorial intervention.
The plays make the case

Milotic's interception came late in the first quarter. Violet already led 6–0. He took Vick's deep-left throw fifty-two yards the other way, and the extra point made it 13–0. That changed the immediate task for an offense already working without DeZhaun Watzon. Sunyshore now needed to recover two scores rather than settle into a competitive game.

The forced fumble mattered in a different way. Nair Jordan caught a short-right pass late in the second quarter and lost the ball. Milotic recovered. Violet's next snap was Iron Jugulis's four-yard touchdown pass to Carnivine. The cornerback didn't score that touchdown himself, but he supplied the possession and the position. Giving him credit requires no imaginative accounting.

He also broke up a third-quarter pass intended for Fera Gatr. The interception and fumble are louder. The breakup belongs in the same account because it shows his afternoon wasn't confined to two unusual moments. He made another ordinary defensive play in a game where Sunyshore would have appreciated one more successful throw.

body.speaker: Milotic
body.text: I didn't take the whole trade onto the field. Just my number. It seemed to be enough luggage.

I like that answer more than any promise of permanent vindication. A player can enjoy this game without predicting the next ten. So can the rest of us. Milotic's performance was exceptional, and Sunyshore will have to live with it. Neither statement needs a claim about what every other player in the exchange will eventually become.
Violet still had to finish

There is another danger in a perfect trade narrative: it can make the winning team's later work disappear. Violet led 26–20 late in the third quarter. The early defensive touchdowns and field position hadn't ended the game. The Falcons still needed to protect a six-point lead against a team that had already scored twenty.

They answered with a 75-yard touchdown drive. A sack made the possession harder. Zangoose converted third-and-ten with an eleven-yard run. Furret caught a 26-yard deep-right pass. Jugulis finished the series with a one-yard run for a touchdown at 4:38. Those plays are part of the victory, too. Milotic gave Violet a remarkable advantage; the offense eventually supplied the drive that made it hold.

Furret finished with seven catches for 147 yards. The completions included gains of 44, 28, 26 and 24. That is a substantial receiving performance to have sharing a headline with a cornerback's reunion. Violet didn't merely wait for the former Starseeker to do everything. It generated its own explosive plays and found a crucial late conversion on the ground.

Sunyshore outgained Violet 286–272, earned more first downs and converted six of twelve third downs to the Falcons' two of seven. Those numbers don't reverse the score. They do help explain why the game remained close enough to require that last long drive. The Starseekers could move the ball. The turnovers made their successful possessions more expensive to replace.
What comes after the headline

At 4–1, Sunyshore still has a very good record. Watzon is clear of the injury report. Veilstone visits next, giving the Starseekers an immediate chance to show how the new roster works with their starting quarterback available again. That is a more useful next test than asking them to defend the trade in the abstract after every practice.

I will watch whether they protect possession and whether their offense finishes drives. I will also watch the roles of the incoming players over time. A transaction's eventual value depends on what a team receives and uses, as well as what it gives away. One spectacular revenge game can't supply all of those answers. It can make the questions much less comfortable.

Violet goes to Mahogany at 2–3, with an opportunity to turn its biggest win into a more sustained recovery. That matters for the Falcons, who are entitled to a story about their own future rather than permanent employment as the supporting cast in Sunyshore's embarrassment. They have Milotic now. They also have a receiver who just gained 147 yards and an offense that finished the decisive drive.

For this week, however, the headline belongs where it belongs. Sunyshore traded Milotic. Milotic helped beat Sunyshore. The longer transaction analysis can wait for more football. The film from this afternoon already has its author.
